description: Hi everyone! I'm Laxmaan, a final-year Biomedical Engineering student at Sathyabama Institute of Science and Technology, India. I'm passionate about the intersection of biomedical engineering, space medicine, human physiology, and technology.
summary:
We developed a systematic data-analysis pipeline to investigate the optical variability of five nearby Seyfert galaxies, a type of Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN), using publicly available observations from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF).

Using Python and Gaussian Process modelling, we retrieved, cleaned, and analysed long-term astronomical light curves to estimate the characteristic damping timescale of each galaxy using the Damped Random Walk (DRW) model. We also performed injection-recovery simulations to evaluate how irregular observation intervals, measurement uncertainties, and limited observation periods could affect the reliability of our results.

Our analysis identified damping timescales ranging from approximately 9.4 to 143 days across the five galaxies. By comparing these measurements, we investigated how optical variability relates to the physical properties of supermassive black holes and their accretion discs.

This project demonstrates how archival astronomical survey data and statistical modelling can help researchers study distant cosmic phenomena that cannot be directly resolved, while providing a reproducible framework for further AGN variability research.
details:
Our project investigates the optical variability of five nearby Seyfert galaxies (NGC 4151, NGC 5548, Mrk 817, NGC 4051 and NGC 7469) to understand the changing behaviour of matter surrounding supermassive black holes.

We developed a reusable Python-based analysis pipeline that retrieves long-term optical light-curve data from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) through the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). The pipeline applies data-quality filtering, removes unreliable measurements, combines observations taken on the same night and models the variability using a Damped Random Walk (DRW), implemented as a Gaussian Process with celerite2. We also used injection-recovery simulations to test how irregular sampling, measurement noise and limited observation periods affect the reliability of the estimated timescales.

The project produced characteristic damping timescales ranging from approximately 9.4 to 143 days across the five galaxies. These measurements provide insight into the variability of AGN accretion discs and their relationship with central black-hole properties.

Our approach is creative in combining archival survey observations, stochastic modelling and target-specific simulations to assess not only the measured variability but also the reliability of the results. We considered data quality, observation cadence, seasonal gaps, measurement uncertainties, viewing geometry and finite observational baselines.

Tools and technologies: Python, Jupyter Notebook, celerite2, Gaussian Process modelling, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, Pandas, Matplotlib and the ZTF/IRSA data services. No physical hardware was required.
